messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The rain had turned the interstate into a slick black mirror when the delivery truck’s tires lost their grip on the on-ramp. Elias Vance remembered the sickening lurch as the trailer swung around, the glass exploding inward like shattered ice, and the sudden, absolute weight of the dashboard pressing against his ribs. He woke up in the wreckage hours later, tangled in seatbelt webbing and airbag dust, listening to the distant wail of sirens and the steady drip of coolant. It took six surgeries to reset his jaw and mend the fractured sternum, but the physical toll was only the beginning. Even now, nearly two years later, Elias understood why a simple glance at a dented fender on a residential street could freeze his breath: he knew exactly how metal groaned before it folded, how the sound of a tire skidding could still trigger a spike of adrenaline that made his hands tremble. He had come to associate the very texture of asphalt with the moment his world had fractured, and that visceral memory made every passing vehicle feel like a suspended threat. As the hospital discharge papers stacked up, a quieter fracture took hold. Elias found himself unable to trust the steady rhythm of his own breathing or the reliability of his legs after long walks. The thought that his body could no longer be depended upon to keep him safe became a constant hum beneath his thoughts. Alongside that came a profound sense of dislocation. He would catch his reflection in a shop window and barely recognize the man staring back, his movements stiff, his expressions flattened by a fatigue that sleep could not touch. He felt like he no longer knew who he was, as if the accident had scraped away the core of his personality and left only a cautious, fragmented shell. The changes, he was certain, were permanent; the man who used to laugh easily at client disagreements or spontaneously take road trips was gone, replaced by someone who measured his days in controlled steps. These internal fractures coincided with the daily demands of his work as an interior designer. His practice relied on client meetings, site visits, and the constant movement between urban storefronts and suburban remodels. When a prospective client began recounting a multi-car pileup on the expressway to describe their fear of driving, Elias felt his pulse jump against his collar. He politely excused himself, citing a scheduling conflict, and spent the next hour in his car down the block, waiting for the tightness in his chest to ease. Later, while reviewing blueprints at his drafting table, a delivery truck backing up outside the studio window made him flinch so violently that his coffee mug slid across the desk. He kept a mental ledger of these moments, not as clinical data, but as reminders of how fragile his tolerance had become. He began declining jobs that required site visits in high-traffic corridors, opting instead for virtual consultations. The loss of in-person client interaction meant a steady decline in his practice’s revenue, but the quiet studio felt safer than the unpredictable streets. The accumulation of these small surrenders eventually made the isolation unbearable. His divorce had been finalized six months into the recovery, and though his ex-wife had been patient, she had confessed that living with a man who seemed perpetually braced for impact was exhausting. Elias had come to believe that continuing down this path would only deepen the gulf between him and anyone he cared about. He finally scheduled an intake, driven by a desperate hope that he might reclaim some of his former spontaneity, even as he feared the therapist would confirm his worst suspicion: that he was permanently changed, broken beyond repair. He sat in the waiting room that morning, staring at the scuffed linoleum, wondering if he could ever learn to sit still in a car again without feeling the steering wheel slip through his grip.
